title: HTA biobank -80°C freezer alarms muted, untested or dependent on campus IT — inspection shortfalls and lost tissue collections
problem: In HTA-licensed research tissue banks, -80°C freezer alarms are muted for weeks, never tested, or their remote dial-out fails because it rides on the university network (published HTA inspection reports cite a muted -80°C alarm and remote alarms blocked by 'IT problems' at UCL Cancer Institute 2023, untested alarms at Broomfield 2018 and New Cross 2013). One weekend failure can destroy years of consented samples (RPI's 2023 lawsuit sought ~$1m over a single freezer), and every shortfall needs a corrective action plan.
who_suffers: Biobank technicians and PIs who lose irreplaceable consented samples; the HTA Designated Individual who owns the shortfall
buyer: HTA Designated Individual / Biobank (Tissue Bank) Manager
industry: HTA-licensed research tissue banks and biobanks in universities, NHS trusts and CROs
current_workaround: Daily manual max/min readings on paper, local audible alarms, legacy BMS or IT-networked monitoring, and monthly 'alarm tests' that often aren't recorded
sensor_concept: Flat-cable PT1000 probe through the door gasket to a mains+battery LTE-M logger with its own SIM (no campus IT); call/SMS escalation tree; firmware-scheduled alarm self-test that requires a human acknowledgement and records it, producing an HTA-ready 'alarm tested and acknowledged' log plus trend plots flagging compressor decline.
notes: Strong c4 (HTA licensing standards + published inspection shortfalls), c1 (sample-loss lawsuits), c2 (daily logs, monthly alarm tests), c8 (cellular, no IT — an HTA report itself cites IT failure). c7 risk: crowded freezer-monitoring market (XiltriX, Rees, Tutela); angle is no-IT + automated alarm-test evidence sold via freezer service engineers.

title: Liquid nitrogen storage dewar boils down between weekly top-ups — cryopreserved cell lines and vials lost
problem: Standalone LN2 dewars in core facilities and biobanks lose nitrogen daily; if a weekly top-up is missed, a lid is left ajar or the vacuum jacket degrades (boil-off rises), vapour-phase temperature climbs and years of cell lines/vials are lost (~£5k–£100k+ to rebuild a cell bank or re-collect samples). Checks are a weekly dipstick reading on a paper log; vacuum failure goes unnoticed until the dewar is empty.
who_suffers: Core facility technicians and PIs whose cell banks are lost
buyer: Core Facility Manager / Lab Manager
industry: University, hospital and CRO cryogenic storage of cell lines and samples
current_workaround: Weekly dipstick level checks with paper logs; LN2 supplier tops up on a fixed schedule; only large auto-fill freezers have controllers
sensor_concept: Low-profile load-cell weighing platform under each dewar (LN2 mass and boil-off rate), LTE-M; alerts on low level, abnormal boil-off (vacuum failure) and missed top-ups; level shared with the LN2 supplier for top-up scheduling; automatic fill log.
notes: c2 (weekly fills/checks), c3 (manual dipping), c6 (BOC/Air Liquide drivers already visit weekly and could bundle it), c8 (load cells are cheap; no O2/ATEX sensing). Risk: c1 needs sourced loss figures; large auto-fill units have built-in controllers.

title: Overnight water-cooled condenser hose pops off — chemistry lab floods the floors below
problem: Chemistry labs leave tap-water condensers running overnight; a hose slipping off a fitting floods the lab and the ceilings and instruments on floors below (a University of Regina safety advisory describes a 4th-floor lab flooding several floors; a Columbia EHS report describes an unattended-experiment leak into floors below). One flood costs ~£10k–£100k+ in damaged instruments, ceilings and lost lab time; universities respond with tagging rules and monthly tubing inspections that researchers ignore.
who_suffers: Researchers and instrument owners on the floors below; building managers; the university insurance team
buyer: Departmental Safety Officer / Chemistry Building or Facilities Manager
industry: University and pharma synthetic chemistry laboratories
current_workaround: Policies requiring hose clamps, overnight tags with phone numbers, monthly tubing inspections, ad hoc purchase of recirculating chillers
sensor_concept: Per-fume-cupboard kit: clip-on flow sensor on the condenser supply, leak tape in the tray/floor and a battery motorised shut-off valve, with a LoRaWAN/LTE-M lab hub (no campus IT). Auto-shuts water on a leak and logs 'unattended overnight water use' per cupboard for EHS policy enforcement.
notes: c10 (multiple university EHS advisories), c3 (tagging/inspection routines), c8 (cheap valves and leak sensors). Weak c2 for floods themselves; the recurring element is nightly unattended running. Channel via estates term contractors or lab distributors is unproven.

title: Lab eyewash stations and emergency showers not flushed weekly — tag cards blank and stagnant water in an emergency
problem: Plumbed eyewash stations and emergency showers should be activated weekly (ANSI Z358.1 in the US; BS EN 15154 guidance; little-used outlets are a Legionella dead-leg under HSG274). Many go unflushed for months, so a casualty gets a face-full of brown, bacteria-laden water, and audits and insurer surveys find blank tag cards. A site with 30–100 stations spends ~1–3 staff hours a week walking round flushing and initialling tags.
who_suffers: Lab users in an emergency; safety officers at audit
buyer: Lab Safety / SHE Manager (universities, pharma, chemical sites)
industry: University, pharma and industrial laboratories with plumbed eyewash/safety showers
current_workaround: Weekly manual flush with tag card or paper log; water hygiene contractor does monthly temperature checks on some outlets
sensor_concept: Strap-on pipe sensor per station (dual thermistor + vibration/acoustic flow detection), LoRaWAN or LTE-M; logs every activation and its duration, flags stations not flushed for 7 days, captures real emergency activations for incident reporting, and exports a weekly compliance sheet.
notes: c2 (weekly mandated task), c3 (labour quantifiable), c4 (ANSI/BS EN/ACoP L8), c6 (water hygiene contractors and eyewash suppliers already visit). c1 is the weak point: the money is labour and injury liability.

title: Fume cupboard sashes left open overnight on older hoods — energy waste and unverified extract between LEV tests
problem: Each ducted fume cupboard exhausts conditioned air around the clock; open sashes on VAV hoods (or failing fans on constant-volume hoods) waste ~£1k–£3k a year per hood in heating, cooling and fan energy. Universities with 200–1,000 hoods run 'shut the sash' campaigns with manual night audits. Older hoods lack airflow indicators, so failing extract goes unnoticed between the 14-monthly COSHH LEV thorough examinations.
who_suffers: Estates energy budgets; researchers exposed when extract falls
buyer: University Energy / Sustainability Manager, with the Lab Facilities Manager
industry: University and pharma laboratories with ducted fume cupboards (older constant-volume and VAV stock)
current_workaround: Sticker campaigns, night-time sash audits by sustainability teams, 14-monthly LEV tests by contractors; BMS-integrated VAV controllers only in new builds
sensor_concept: Retrofit clip-on sash-height sensor (ToF or magnetic) plus a small differential-pressure/thermal airflow sensor at the hood, LoRaWAN/LTE-M; nightly 'sash open' alerts and per-lab league tables, low-airflow alarm, and a running log supporting COSHH Reg 9 records between LEV tests.
notes: c1 (energy £ quantifiable), c2 (nightly), c3 (manual audits), c4 (COSHH LEV / HSG258), c6 (LEV test contractors visit every 14 months). Risk: BMS/VAV incumbents in new buildings; target older stock.

title: CO2 cylinder feeding cell-culture incubators runs out over the weekend — weeks of cultures lost
problem: Single-cylinder or manually switched CO2 supplies to cell-culture incubators run dry on a Friday night; by Monday the media pH has drifted and cultures (primary cells, organoids, weeks of work) are lost, ~£2k–£20k per event in reagents and staff time. Cylinder changes and stock checks are a weekly manual chore and incubator alarms go unheard at weekends.
who_suffers: Researchers and tissue-culture technicians
buyer: Lab Manager / Tissue Culture Facility Manager
industry: University, hospital and biotech cell-culture laboratories
current_workaround: Weekly cylinder pressure checks, manual changeover manifolds, incubator local alarms
sensor_concept: Inline pressure transducer on the cylinder manifold (or weighing plate under cylinders) plus incubator inlet pressure, LTE-M; low-gas and 'changeover happened' alerts, consumption trends, automatic notice to the gas supplier for a replacement cylinder, weekly gas log.
notes: c2 (weekly cylinder changes), c3 (manual checks), c6 (industrial gas suppliers deliver weekly), c8 (pressure transducers cheap). Risk: supplier digital cylinders and auto-changeover panels compete; c4 modest.

title: Animal facility room temperature, humidity and light-cycle excursions — ASPA records kept by hand and transgenic lines at risk
problem: Home Office-designated establishments must keep animal rooms within the Code of Practice ranges and record conditions; technicians read min/max thermohygrometers daily and write on door sheets. A failed HVAC or stuck light timer overnight can stress or kill rodents and invalidate studies, and losing a unique transgenic line costs ~£5k–£30k to rederive plus study write-offs. Inspectors expect records and out-of-hours alarms, which often go to estates rather than animal staff.
who_suffers: Animal technicians, the NACWO, researchers whose studies are invalidated
buyer: Animal Facility Manager / Named Animal Care & Welfare Officer (NACWO)
industry: UK university and CRO animal units (rodent, zebrafish) under ASPA
current_workaround: Daily manual min/max readings per room on paper; BMS alarms routed to estates; spot checks of light timers
sensor_concept: Per-room battery sensor measuring temperature, RH, lux (verifies the light/dark cycle timing) and optionally noise, LTE-M (no campus IT); alerts to the on-call technician, automatic daily record sheets per room, audit export for inspectors.
notes: c2 (daily manual task), c4 (ASPA Code of Practice), c5 (NACWO/facility manager are named statutory roles), c9 (statutory records). Risk: BMS incumbents and slow university procurement.

title: GP-surgery blood samples left in cold collection boxes and vans — spurious high potassium, rejected samples and patient recalls
problem: Blood samples collected at GP surgeries wait in collection boxes and courier vans at uncontrolled temperatures. Winter cold causes seasonal pseudohyperkalaemia (spuriously high potassium) and summer heat degrades samples, triggering repeat bleeds, unnecessary urgent referrals and wasted tests (~£20–£50 per repeat, far more per unnecessary admission). Labs see it weekly in season but cannot show where in the chain it failed.
who_suffers: Patients recalled; GP practice staff; laboratory biomedical scientists
buyer: Pathology Network Logistics / Quality Manager (ISO 15189-accredited lab)
industry: NHS and private pathology sample collection and courier networks
current_workaround: Insulated bags, occasional data-logger audits, lab rejection rules, phoning surgeries
sensor_concept: Rugged temperature + lid-open/light sensor in each surgery collection box and courier bag, LTE-M; per-run temperature trace keyed to a QR label on the box (no LIMS integration), excursion alerts to the courier, monthly ISO 15189 pre-analytical quality report.
notes: c2 (daily runs), c10 (peer-reviewed literature on seasonal pseudohyperkalaemia), c4 (ISO 15189 pre-analytical requirements). Risks: c5 NHS procurement speed; channel via courier contractors.

title: Plant growth rooms and controlled-environment chambers fail silently at the weekend — season-long experiments lost
problem: Plant science and agri-tech research relies on growth rooms holding temperature, light and CO2 for months; a failed lighting contactor or chiller over a weekend can wipe out a season-long experiment or a breeding generation (~£10k–£100k of research time and grant money). Controller alarms are local, and staff do daily walk-round checks.
who_suffers: Plant scientists, PhD students, research technicians
buyer: Controlled Environment / Glasshouse Facility Manager
industry: University plant-science departments, agri-tech research institutes and plant breeders
current_workaround: Daily walk-round checks, manual download of chamber controller logs, BMS alarms routed to estates
sensor_concept: Independent watchdog per chamber: temperature, RH, PAR/lux, NDIR CO2 and door-open, LTE-M; alerts on deviation from the programmed setpoints and photoperiod, plus an independent experiment-conditions log for publications and reviewers.
notes: c3 (daily walk-rounds), c8 (NDIR CO2 ~£20–£30), niche underserved by generic monitors. Weaker c4 (research integrity rather than regulation); c1/c2 moderate.

title: Holiday-park lodge hot tubs tested by hand at every changeover — HSG282 logs patchy and Legionella risk
problem: Holiday parks and glamping sites with dozens to hundreds of lodge hot tubs must control Legionella under HSE's HSG282, which covers domestic-type hot tubs used in a business such as holiday-park rentals: frequent disinfectant/pH checks and records. Staff test by hand between guests and logs are patchy. Hot-tub-linked outbreaks lead to closures, enforcement and compensation claims; manual testing takes ~10–20 minutes per tub per day.
who_suffers: Guests (illness), housekeeping and maintenance staff, park managers
buyer: Holiday Park Operations / Maintenance Manager (multi-lodge operators)
industry: Holiday parks, lodge resorts and glamping sites with lodge hot tubs (UK)
current_workaround: Test strips or photometers at each changeover with paper logs; weekly visits from a hot-tub service contractor; council guidance letters
sensor_concept: Floating or inline probe pod (ORP for disinfectant, pH, temperature) with replaceable probes, LTE-M; flags tubs out of range before guest arrival, auto-builds the HSG282 log per tub, alerts on heater/pump failure; service-contractor dashboard.
notes: c4 (HSG282 + council enforcement), c2 (daily), c3 (manual testing labour), c6 (hot-tub service contractors visit weekly). Risk c8: ORP/pH probe drift and cost (~£20–£40 per probe) need proven calibration life.

title: Pool dosing-chemical drum runs dry overnight — disinfectant drops and the pool can't open in the morning
problem: Leisure centre, hotel and school pools dose sodium hypochlorite and acid from drums or IBCs. When a drum runs dry overnight, disinfectant falls and the pool fails its pre-opening test (lost sessions and swim-school refunds, ~£1k–£5k a day for a busy leisure pool), and the emergency delivery costs extra. Staff check drum levels by eye; chemical suppliers deliver on fixed rounds.
who_suffers: Duty managers, swimmers, swim schools
buyer: Leisure Centre / Pool Plant Manager (or hotel Chief Engineer), via the chemical supply contract
industry: Commercial pools: leisure trusts, hotels and schools
current_workaround: Visual drum checks on daily plant-room rounds, fixed-schedule deliveries, emergency call-outs
sensor_concept: Weighing platform under drums/IBCs (or ultrasonic level in an IBC) plus dosing-pump pulse/current monitoring, LTE-M; low-stock and 'dosing stopped' alerts, consumption trends (detects over-dosing or leaks), feed to supplier auto-replenishment.
notes: c6 strong (pool chemical distributors visit regularly and could offer vendor-managed inventory), c2 (daily rounds), c8 (load cells cheap, no ATEX). c1 needs sourced closure costs.

title: Pool chemical delivered into the wrong tank — acid meets hypochlorite and chlorine gas evacuates the building
problem: HSE has said accidental addition of acid to hypochlorite is the commonest cause of chlorine releases in pool buildings. Wrong-tank deliveries and mixing have hospitalised bathers and led to prosecutions (Sheffield Springs £7k; Nuffield Health and Honeywell £45k each; Virgin Active Omni £20k; David Lloyd £70k plus £60k costs in a chloramine case), plus evacuation and closure costs. Every delivery (weekly or fortnightly) should be supervised, with locked, labelled fill points, and often isn't.
who_suffers: Bathers and staff exposed to gas; plant operators prosecuted
buyer: Leisure Trust Health & Safety Manager / Head of Operations
industry: Public and private swimming pools using bulk liquid chemicals
current_workaround: Colour-coded fill points, padlocks, supervised-delivery procedures, delivery paperwork
sensor_concept: Smart fill-point lock on each tank (keypad/RFID unlock matched to the delivery note's chemical), lock-state and hose-connection sensor, tank level change confirming which tank received product, LTE-M; logs every delivery (who, when, which tank, volume) and alarms if a fill point opens without matching authorisation.
notes: c4/c10 (HSE prosecutions, HSG179), c1 (fines + closures), c2 (weekly deliveries as a recurring supervised task), c6 (chemical suppliers + pool plant contractors). Risk: value is catastrophe-driven; sell it as the delivery-supervision record.

title: Pool circulation pump trips or heater fails overnight — water quality and temperature fail and the pool stays shut
problem: When a circulation pump trips, a strainer blocks or the heat exchanger fails overnight, turnover stops and disinfectant and temperature drift; the pool fails pre-opening tests and closes for the day (lost revenue and lessons, ~£1k–£5k a day) and needs an emergency engineer. Plant rooms are unmanned at night, and smaller pools in hotels and schools have no BMS alarms.
who_suffers: Duty managers, hotel guests, swim schools
buyer: Hotel Chief Engineer / Leisure Pool Plant Manager
industry: Hotel, school and smaller leisure pools without full BMS
current_workaround: Plant-room rounds at opening and closing with a paper log; reactive maintenance contractor call-outs
sensor_concept: Clamp-on CT on the circulation pump plus pipe vibration, strap-on flow/return temperatures on the heat exchanger and a plant-room flood sensor, LTE-M; out-of-hours alerts, auto-filled daily plant log, pump-health trend for the maintenance contractor.
notes: c2 (daily plant rounds), c3, c6 (pool maintenance contractors on monthly service contracts), c8 (CTs and thermistors cheap). c4 moderate (PWTAG plant records).

title: Pool sand filters backwashed by habit, not need — thousands of litres of heated, treated water dumped every week
problem: Pool sand filters are backwashed on fixed days rather than on pressure differential. Each backwash dumps ~10–30 m³ of heated, chemically treated water (water, sewerage, heat and chemicals at roughly £5–£10/m³, so ~£100–£300 a time), while under-backwashing raises turbidity and Cryptosporidium risk. Operators log backwashes by hand.
who_suffers: Leisure trust utility budgets; pool plant operators
buyer: Leisure Trust Energy / Facilities Manager; Pool Plant Manager
industry: Leisure centre and hotel pools with sand or media filtration
current_workaround: Fixed weekly backwash schedule, reading analogue pressure gauges, paper logbooks
sensor_concept: Pressure sensors on filter inlet and outlet plus clamp-on flow detection on the backwash line, LTE-M; tells operators when a backwash is genuinely due, records each backwash duration and volume, calculates water and energy dumped, exports a PWTAG-style log.
notes: c1 (utility costs quantifiable), c2 (weekly), c3 (manual logs), c8 (pressure sensors ~£10–£20). c4 moderate (PWTAG guidance only).

title: Pool cover left off overnight — leisure centre heat and dehumidification energy burned for nothing
problem: An uncovered indoor pool loses most of its heat by evaporation overnight, and the pool-hall air-handling units run hard to remove the moisture. Leisure operators facing energy bills of £100k+ per site have installed covers, but staff skip deploying them at closing. Each uncovered night wastes ~£20–£100 of energy per pool, and managers have no evidence of whether covers were used.
who_suffers: Leisure operator energy budgets; council and leisure trust net-zero targets
buyer: Leisure Trust Energy / Sustainability Manager
industry: Indoor leisure centre, school and hotel pools with covers
current_workaround: Closing checklists, occasional night spot checks, energy dashboards with no cover data
sensor_concept: Rotation/tilt sensor on the cover roller (or a float/ToF sensor detecting the cover on the water) plus pool-hall temperature/RH, LTE-M; nightly 'cover not deployed' alert to the duty manager, monthly covered-hours vs energy report, evidence for energy-grant schemes.
notes: c1 (energy savings sourceable via Sport England / Carbon Trust guidance), c2 (nightly), c6 (pool cover suppliers/installers already service sites). c4 weak: value is energy.

title: Swim schools renting hotel pools arrive to find the water too cold — lessons cancelled and refunds paid
problem: Baby and children's swim-school franchisees rent hotel, school and private pools; hosts let the water drift below the ~30–32°C that baby classes need, or out of chemical range. Teachers find out on arrival, classes are cancelled (~£300–£1,000 per session in refunds and make-ups) and franchise welfare standards are breached. Franchisees have no data to hold pool owners to the hire agreement.
who_suffers: Swim-school teachers and franchisees; parents and babies
buyer: Swim School Franchise Owner / Franchisor Operations Director
industry: Baby and children's swim-school franchises renting third-party pools
current_workaround: Teacher checks a thermometer on arrival, phone calls to pool owners, written hire agreements
sensor_concept: Small floating or clip-on temperature sensor left in the pool (optional ORP), LTE-M; early-morning alert if water is below the contracted temperature so classes can be moved, monthly compliance report to share with the pool owner and franchisor.
notes: c5 strong (franchisees with defined budgets), c6 (franchisor HQ as channel), c2 (weekly sessions), distinct buyer. c4 weak-moderate (franchise standards, not law).

title: Gym and hotel-spa sauna heaters left on overnight — fire risk and wasted energy
problem: Gym and hotel-spa sauna heaters (6–12 kW) are often left on after closing or have timers overridden. Sauna fires are a recurring claim in leisure premises, and a heater left on all night burns ~£20–£40 of electricity. Closing checklists are the only control.
who_suffers: Gym and spa operators, insurers, neighbouring units
buyer: Gym / Spa General Manager or Facilities Manager; insurer risk engineer
industry: Budget and independent gyms and hotel spas with saunas and steam rooms
current_workaround: Closing checklists, mechanical timers, occasional insurer survey recommendations
sensor_concept: Clamp-on current sensor on the sauna heater supply plus a high-temperature thermistor at the ceiling, LTE-M; alert if the heater is on outside opening hours or the temperature exceeds a safe limit; closing-check record and energy report for the insurer.
notes: c2 (nightly closing task), c6 (insurer surveys, spa equipment service contractors), c8 (CT clamps cheap). c1/c4 need insurer evidence on sauna fire claims.

title: Little-used pool and spa changing-room showers — weekly Legionella flushing and monthly temperature checks done by hand
problem: Leisure centres and spas have dozens of showers and TMVs. ACoP L8 / HSG274 requires little-used outlets to be flushed weekly and sentinel temperatures to be checked monthly, so duty staff walk round flushing and water-hygiene contractors charge per outlet to take temperatures. Records are often incomplete, which is a recurring theme in HSE Legionella enforcement.
who_suffers: Duty staff doing flushing rounds; the Legionella responsible person
buyer: Leisure Trust Compliance / Facilities Manager (Legionella responsible person)
industry: Leisure centre, gym and spa changing rooms
current_workaround: Weekly flushing rounds by staff with paper logs; monthly temperature checks by a water-hygiene contractor
sensor_concept: Strap-on dual pipe thermistors on each shower/TMV supply detect use and record hot/cold temperatures, LoRaWAN or LTE-M gateway; auto-identifies outlets unused for 7 days (only those need flushing), logs sentinel temperatures continuously, exports an L8 compliance record.
notes: c4 (ACoP L8, HSE enforcement), c2 (weekly), c3 (staff and contractor labour quantifiable), c6 (water-hygiene contractors). c7 risk: Legionella-monitoring vendors exist; the angle is the pool/spa niche.

title: Hired site welfare units serviced on a fixed weekly round — waste tanks overflow or water runs out between visits
problem: Construction sites must provide toilets and washing water (CDM 2015 Schedule 2). Hire companies service welfare units weekly at ~£65–£120 a visit, so busy sites overflow or run dry mid-week (emergency call-outs, angry customers, welfare breaches) while quiet sites get visits they don't need.
who_suffers: Site workers without toilets or water; site managers; hire service drivers
buyer: Hire company Welfare / Service Operations Manager
industry: Welfare unit and site accommodation hire
current_workaround: Fixed weekly servicing schedule, customer phone calls for extra visits, drivers checking tanks on arrival
sensor_concept: Ultrasonic level sensor on the waste tank, level/pressure on the fresh-water tank, weight on the gas bottle and generator run-hours, LTE-M; dynamic service routing (empty at ~80% full), pre-overflow alerts, proof of service and CDM welfare records for the contractor.
notes: c3 (quantified per-visit service costs), c2 (weekly), c4 (CDM Schedule 2 welfare duty), c5/c6 (the hire company is both buyer and channel), c8 (ultrasonic level sensors cheap).

title: Small hired plant sits idle on site for weeks — off-hire disputes and wasted hire spend
problem: Contractors forget to off-hire breakers, pumps, compressors and generators. CPA model conditions keep charges running until the kit is formally off-hired and collected, so plant sits idle for weeks and disputes erupt over when it was 'called off' (guides advise a dated off-hire reference because 'a phone call to the depot does not stop the meter'). Large plant has OEM telematics; small hired kit does not.
who_suffers: Contractor site managers and QS teams; hire desk staff handling disputes
buyer: Contractor Plant / Procurement Manager, or hire company Operations Director (as a service)
industry: Small plant and tool hire to construction and utility contractors
current_workaround: Weekly on-hire reports, manual site walk-rounds, paper off-hire numbers, disputed invoices
sensor_concept: Rugged tag with an accelerometer (running vibration gives daily use hours) and GPS, LTE-M, multi-year battery; weekly 'idle more than 3 days' report per site for the contractor, timestamped location and use evidence for off-hire disputes, utilisation data for the hire company.
notes: c1 (hire spend £ quantifiable), c2 (weekly), c3 (manual on-hire reconciliation), c6 (hire companies as channel). c7 risk: crowded tracker market; differentiate on idle time and dispute evidence for small plant.

title: Hired breakers and grinders used without real trigger-time records — HAVS prosecutions with £100k+ fines
problem: Employers must assess and control hand-arm vibration exposure under the Control of Vibration at Work Regulations 2005, and HSE regularly prosecutes (Stonewater £140k, a car dealership £200k+, Places for People £600k). Most vibrating tools on sites are hired, and hirers rely on paper estimates of trigger time; dedicated HAV monitoring systems are expensive and don't move with hired tools.
who_suffers: Operatives developing HAVS; site supervisors and H&S managers
buyer: Contractor Health & Safety Manager, sold as a hire-desk add-on by the hire company
industry: Tool hire for construction, utilities, groundworks and facilities maintenance
current_workaround: Paper HAV points calculators, supervisor estimates, some wearable HAV monitors, health surveillance after the fact
sensor_concept: Bolt-on tag fitted by the hire depot to each vibrating tool: accelerometer measures actual trigger time and vibration level, BLE to the operative's card/phone or LTE-M direct; per-operative daily exposure points against EAV/ELV, alert at the action value, records for HSE.
notes: c4/c10 strong (HSE prosecutions under statutory regs), c1 (fines + civil claims), c2 (daily use), c6 (hire companies fit and service tools). c7 risk: Reactec/HAVi incumbents; the gap is the hire-fleet-embedded model.

title: Portable traffic signals at street works go dark or get knocked over at night — gridlock, overrun charges and permit breaches
problem: Portable traffic lights at roadworks run on batteries or solar. When a head goes dark, is knocked over or loses sync at night, traffic backs up, accident risk rises and the highway authority can levy Section 74 overrun charges or permit-condition penalties (often hundreds to thousands of pounds a day). Operators currently find out from the public.
who_suffers: Street works contractors, motorists, traffic management crews
buyer: Traffic Management Hire Company Operations Manager; utility contractor Street Works Manager
industry: Temporary traffic management hire for utility and highway works
current_workaround: Scheduled battery swaps, daily drive-by inspections, public calls to helplines
sensor_concept: Retrofit module per signal head measuring battery voltage, lamp current, tilt/shock and GPS, LTE-M; alerts on lamp failure, low battery, knock-over or movement; inspection log for NRSWA and permit-scheme compliance.
notes: c2 (daily inspections), c3 (drive-by checks), c4 (NRSWA, permit schemes), c6 (TM hire companies). c7 risk: newer OEM signals have telemetry; target retrofit of existing fleets.

title: Hired temporary fencing panels blown over or unclipped overnight — site perimeter open to the public
problem: Construction and utility sites rely on hired mesh fencing; wind or intruders knock panels over or unclip them at night, exposing excavations to the public (CDM duty to prevent unauthorised access; occupiers' liability) and enabling theft. Site teams discover it the next morning, and fencing hire firms are called out to re-erect it.
who_suffers: Site managers; members of the public (especially children) entering sites; fencing hire crews
buyer: Contractor Site / Project Manager; fencing hire company as reseller
industry: Temporary fencing hire for construction, utilities and events
current_workaround: Daily perimeter walks, security patrols, CCTV towers on bigger sites
sensor_concept: Clip-on tilt, shock and 'clamp opened' magnetic sensor on every Nth panel and at gates, LoRaWAN gateway with LTE-M backhaul on site; immediate alert to the keyholder or security when panels fall or gates open out of hours; daily perimeter-integrity log.
notes: c4 (CDM site security duty), c2 (daily checks), c6 (fencing hire firms), c8 (cheap accelerometers). c1 needs sourced claim figures for public injury/theft.

title: Steel road plates over trenches shift under traffic — cyclist and motorcyclist injury claims against utility contractors
problem: Road plates over trenches move or rock under HGVs, creating lips and gaps that throw cyclists and motorcyclists; injury claims (~£10k–£100k+), council defect notices and NRSWA signing, lighting and guarding breaches follow. Contractors must inspect street works regularly, but plates move between inspections, often overnight.
who_suffers: Road users; utility contractors and their insurers
buyer: Utility contractor Street Works / SHE Manager; road plate hire company
industry: Road plate and trench cover hire for utility and highway contractors
current_workaround: Periodic inspection visits, pinning and ramping plates, reactive repairs after complaints
sensor_concept: Bolt-on puck on each plate with an accelerometer for displacement, rocking and tilt, plus GPS, LTE-M or LoRaWAN; alert when a plate shifts or rocks beyond threshold; timestamped inspection evidence for claims defence.
notes: c1 (personal injury claim values), c4 (NRSWA Safety at Street Works code of practice), c6 (plate hire and TM firms), c8. c2 moderate (daily inspection regime).

title: Flood-restoration drying kit — insurers dispute run days, homeowners claim electricity and daily moisture visits pile up
problem: After escape-of-water claims, restoration contractors deploy dehumidifiers and air movers for 1–4 weeks. Insurers query whether the kit actually ran and when drying was achieved, homeowners claim electricity reimbursement (~£5–£15 a day per unit), and contractors make daily or alternate-day site visits to take moisture readings. Escape of water is one of the UK's largest home insurance claim categories.
who_suffers: Restoration contractors, loss adjusters, homeowners
buyer: Restoration Contractor Operations Director; insurer claims supply-chain manager
industry: Insurance flood and escape-of-water drying and restoration (drying equipment hire)
current_workaround: Frequent site visits for moisture readings, manual drying logs, estimated electricity payments
sensor_concept: Inline power-logging plug per drying unit, ambient T/RH sensor and an optional wall moisture-pin sensor, with an LTE-M hub; remote drying curve, run-hours and kWh per unit, drying certificate, fewer site visits.
notes: c1/c10 (ABI escape-of-water claims data), c2/c3 (frequent site visits), c6 (insurer supply chains and restoration networks already deploy kit), c9 (per-claim subscription). c7 risk: some drying telemetry exists.

title: Hired generators and lighting towers run dry or get siphoned overnight — dark sites, idle crews and emergency refuels
problem: Hired diesel generators, lighting towers and site heaters on remote sites run out of fuel or are siphoned overnight. Highway night works lose lighting (work stops, crews idle at ~£2k–£10k a night) and emergency fuel deliveries cost a premium. Newer units have OEM telematics, but mixed fleets and older kit don't.
who_suffers: Site managers, night-shift crews, hire company service desks
buyer: Hire company Power & Lighting Division Manager; contractor Plant Manager
industry: Generator, lighting tower and heater hire to construction, highways and events
current_workaround: Manual dipping on site visits, fixed refuel schedules from fuel suppliers, reactive call-outs
sensor_concept: Non-invasive ultrasonic level sensor on the fuel tank top, run/voltage detection, GPS and a tamper/cap-open switch, LTE-M; low-fuel and sudden-drop (theft) alerts, refuel routing for the fuel partner, run-hours for servicing.
notes: c2 (weekly refuels), c3 (manual dips), c6 (hire companies + fuel delivery partners), c8 (diesel is not an ATEX hazard; sensors cheap). c7 risk: OEM telematics on new units.

title: Hired dewatering pump stops overnight — excavation floods, trench sides slump and the programme slips
problem: Groundworks and pipeline excavations rely on hired submersible or diesel pumps. A blocked strainer, tripped supply or empty fuel tank overnight floods the dig, destabilises trench sides and costs a day or more of crew time (~£2k–£10k) plus pumping out. Site teams only check at the start of the shift.
who_suffers: Groundworks crews and site managers
buyer: Groundworks Contractor Contracts / Plant Manager; pump hire company
industry: Pump hire for construction dewatering, utilities and flood response
current_workaround: Start- and end-of-shift checks, night watchmen on critical jobs, float switches with local beacons
sensor_concept: Pressure-type water-level sensor in the sump, pump run detection (vibration or current clamp) and GPS, LTE-M; alert when the pump stops or the level rises; run log for hire billing.
notes: c1 (crew downtime), c2 (daily checks), c6 (pump hire specialists), c8. c4 moderate (CDM excavation inspection duties).

title: Hired scaffolds: 7-day and post-storm statutory inspections done by driving round — tie and base movement missed
problem: The Work at Height Regulations 2005 require scaffold inspections at least every 7 days and after adverse weather. Scaffold contractors drive round dozens of sites to inspect and tag, and a storm triggers hundreds of extra inspections at once. Movement of ties or sole boards between inspections leads to collapses (HSE prosecutions, ~£100k+ fines and claims).
who_suffers: Scaffold inspectors; site workers; the public below
buyer: Scaffolding Contractor Operations Director / Contracts Manager
industry: Scaffold hire and erection contractors
current_workaround: Weekly physical inspections with tags and paper registers; post-storm inspection blitzes
sensor_concept: Clamp-on tilt/accelerometer sensors on key standards and tie points, plus a site wind-gust sensor, LoRaWAN/LTE-M; alerts on movement, local wind records to decide which scaffolds truly need a post-storm inspection, digital inspection register.
notes: c4 (WAHR 2005 Schedule 7 statutory inspections), c2 (weekly), c3 (inspector labour quantifiable), c10 (HSE collapse prosecutions). Risk: law still requires a physical inspection, so the sensor triages rather than replaces it.

title: Licensed glue-board use in England — traps must be checked every few hours unless remotely monitored
problem: Since the Glue Traps (Offences) Act 2022, pest controllers in England may only use glue boards under licence. BPCA guidance on the licence says traps must be inspected at least every ~6 hours (and triggered traps dealt with quickly), with technicians staying on site unless remote monitoring is used. That forces repeat returns (~£50–£100 per extra visit) for mouse infestations in hospitals, food premises and care homes.
who_suffers: Pest technicians making overnight returns; clients waiting; trapped rodents (welfare)
buyer: Pest Control Company Owner / Technical Manager
industry: Professional pest control in England (BPCA/NPTA members)
current_workaround: Technicians staying on site or returning every few hours; avoiding glue boards altogether
sensor_concept: Glue-board holder with a capture sensor (IR beam, capacitive or weight change) and LTE-M (no client Wi-Fi); instant capture alert, timestamped inspection and response log that satisfies licence record-keeping.
notes: c4 strong (statutory licence conditions), c2/c3 (checks every few hours), c6 (Killgerm/1env distributors and BPCA), c9 (per-job rental). Verify the licence wording on remote monitoring.

title: Live-catch cage traps must be physically checked every day — keepers and rangers drive hours round empty traps
problem: Larsen/corvid, grey squirrel and mink cage traps used under the general licences must be physically inspected at least once a day. Keepers, forestry rangers and red-squirrel groups drive for hours each day to check mostly empty traps (~1–3 hours a day per keeper), and a missed check is an animal-welfare offence.
who_suffers: Gamekeepers, forestry rangers, conservation volunteers
buyer: Estate Head Keeper / Estate Manager; forestry or conservation trust project manager
industry: Game estates, forestry and conservation trapping (UK)
current_workaround: Daily driving rounds, written trap logs, a few supplier trap tags
sensor_concept: Door-closed magnetic/tilt sensor and motion sensor on each trap, LoRaWAN or LTE-M (satellite where there is no coverage); capture alerts so animals are dispatched or released quickly; daily inspection log.
notes: c2/c3 (daily mandated checks), c4 (general licence conditions), c10 (welfare prosecutions). Risks c7/c8: Perdix and others already sell trap tags, remote alerts don't legally replace inspection, and rural coverage is poor.

title: Independent pest controllers lose food-factory contracts to the big firms' 'digital' rodent monitoring
problem: BRCGS- and retailer-audited food sites increasingly expect 24/7 digital rodent monitoring. Big players bundle proprietary systems; independent contractors (most of the UK market) can't, and lose contracts worth ~£2k–£20k a year each. Routine visits (roughly 8–12 a year plus call-outs) still involve opening every station.
who_suffers: Independent pest control firms; food-site technical managers paying for visits
buyer: Independent Pest Control Company Owner (resold to the Food Site Technical Manager)
industry: Independent pest control firms servicing BRCGS food manufacturers and warehouses
current_workaround: Manual station checks on every routine visit, paper or app bait records, non-toxic monitoring blocks
sensor_concept: Retrofit sensor for standard bait/monitoring stations and snap traps (IR/capacitive activity plus lid/trigger detection), LoRaWAN gateway with LTE-M backhaul (no client IT); white-label portal that independents can resell; BRCGS-ready trend reports.
notes: c4 (BRCGS pest control clause), c6 (pest-product distributors serve independents), c9 (per-station monthly fee), c7 (enterprise incumbents prove willingness to pay; the gap is independents). Risk: crowded.

title: Rats entering kitchens and flats through defective drains — repeated call-outs until the drain route is proven and closed
problem: Rats in kitchens, hotels and housing blocks often come from defective drains; pest controllers bait inside repeatedly (each call-out ~£100–£300) while the actual route stays open. Fitting non-return rat flaps works, but proving the drain was the route, and that the flap is working, needs repeated CCTV and drain surveys.
who_suffers: Restaurants, hotels and landlords with recurring infestations; pest technicians
buyer: Pest Control Company (drain-rat service), selling to Facilities / Housing Managers
industry: Drain-rat pest control for commercial kitchens, hotels and social housing blocks
current_workaround: Repeated internal baiting, drain CCTV surveys, smoke testing, fitting rat flaps
sensor_concept: Sensor in the manhole or on the rat flap: flap-opening counter (magnetic/tilt) and IR activity, LoRaWAN/LTE-M with the antenna under the cover; proves rat traffic in the drain, verifies the flap after install, alerts if activity returns.
notes: c2 (recurring infestations), c3 (repeat call-outs), c6 (pest/drainage contractors), c7 (niche). c8 risk: RF from under manhole covers; c1 needs sourced figures.

title: Bed bug heat treatments in hotels — no proof every zone reached lethal temperature, so retreatments and refund disputes follow
problem: Hotels pay ~£500–£2,000+ per room for bed bug heat treatment and lose room nights. When bugs return, hotel and contractor argue over whether lethal temperature (~50–60°C held for hours) was reached inside mattresses and furniture voids. Contractors place a few thermometers and check by hand.
who_suffers: Hotel housekeeping and GMs; guests (bites, reviews); pest contractors
buyer: Pest Control Company Owner (heat-treatment service); end client Hotel Group Head of Housekeeping / Operations
industry: Bed bug heat treatment for hotels, hostels and HMOs
current_workaround: Handheld IR thermometers and a few probe loggers downloaded after the job
sensor_concept: Kit of reusable wireless probe sensors (thermistor on a cable into mattresses and voids) with an LTE-M hub; live heat map of all zones, cold-spot alerts, auto-generated 'proof of kill' certificate per room for the hotel and its insurer.
notes: c1 (treatment and lost room-night costs), c3 (manual probe checks), c9 (per-job or subscription), c10 (hotel bed bug complaints and reviews). c7 risk: US vendors (Monnit, AKCP) sell generic kits.

title: Insect light traps switched off or running on dead UV tubes in food factories — auditors find non-functional units
problem: Food factories rely on electric fly killers and insect light traps, but UV output falls substantially within about a year, staff unplug units, and catch trays aren't analysed. BRCGS and retailer audits raise non-conformances, and fly contamination complaints cost money per incident. Tubes are changed on an annual schedule rather than when needed.
who_suffers: Food-site technical and QA teams; pest contractors
buyer: Food Site Technical / QA Manager (through the pest contractor)
industry: Food manufacturing, food retail back-of-house and distribution
current_workaround: Annual tube changes, catch-tray counts on routine visits, manual 'is it on' checks
sensor_concept: Clip-in UV-A photodiode and power/current sensing per unit (optional low-resolution catch-tray image), LoRaWAN/LTE-M; alerts when units are off or UV output degrades, fly-activity trends, BRCGS evidence.
notes: c2 (continuous and per-visit checks), c4 (BRCGS pest control requirements), c6 (pest contractors service the units), c8 (UV photodiodes ~£2–£5). c1 needs sourcing.

title: Birds trapped inside food distribution centres — contaminated stock and audit failures found only when droppings appear
problem: Pigeons, sparrows and starlings get into food DCs and warehouses through dock doors. Droppings contaminate stock and racking (product write-offs and retailer audit non-conformances), and pest firms spend days on bird removal. Infestations are found only when staff notice droppings.
who_suffers: Warehouse managers, food safety teams, pest technicians
buyer: Distribution Centre General Manager / Site Food Safety Manager (through the pest contractor)
industry: Food and grocery distribution centres and large warehouses
current_workaround: Netting and proofing, periodic pest inspections, staff reports
sensor_concept: Battery acoustic sensors high in the racking with an on-device bird-call classifier (TinyML) plus PIR, LoRaWAN/LTE-M; alert on the first bird present and its location, activity log for audits and proofing ROI.
notes: c1 (stock write-offs), c6 (pest contractors already do bird control), c4 (BRCGS Storage & Distribution). c8 risk: acoustic classification accuracy; novel.

title: Farm rodenticide stewardship — CRRU and Red Tractor demand bait inspection records that farmers don't keep
problem: Farmers using professional rodenticides must follow CRRU stewardship: permanent outdoor baiting needs documented justification and re-inspection at least every 4 weeks, and farm assurance (Red Tractor pest control standards) audits the records. Rats also cost farms money every year in feed loss and contamination. Records are routinely missing or back-filled at audit.
who_suffers: Livestock and arable farmers at audit; wildlife (secondary poisoning)
buyer: Farmer / Farm Manager (assured farms)
industry: Assured livestock and arable farms using rodenticides
current_workaround: Paper bait plans and inspection logs filled in before audits; contract pest controllers on some farms
sensor_concept: Bait-station activity sensor (IR/lid) with a bait-consumption estimate, LoRaWAN/LTE-M; auto inspection and activity log in CRRU/Red Tractor format, alert when bait is taken so pulsed baiting can be timed.
notes: c4 (CRRU code + Red Tractor), c2 (4-weekly or more often), c6 (agricultural merchants sell rodenticides with CRRU point-of-sale checks), c9 (audit records). c5: farmer budgets are thin.

title: Food factory external doors propped open — the main pest ingress route that pest reports and auditors keep citing
problem: Dock and fire doors propped open in food factories let in rodents, birds and flies. Pest contractors flag it in service reports and BRCGS audits cite it, but nobody can show how long the doors stand open. Infestation incidents cost ~£k–£100k+ in product disposal and customer complaints.
who_suffers: Food-site technical managers; pest contractors
buyer: Food Site Technical Manager (through the pest contractor's proofing service)
industry: Food manufacturing and food distribution sites
current_workaround: Signage, strip curtains, door closers, pest contractor observations
sensor_concept: Magnetic/accelerometer door-open sensor with a dwell timer and local buzzer, LoRaWAN/LTE-M; alert when a door stays open for more than N minutes, weekly 'open hours by door' report correlated with pest activity.
notes: c4 (BRCGS proofing requirements), c6 (pest contractors already report proofing issues), c8 (trivial BOM). c7 risk: generic door sensors are cheap; the value is integration with the pest programme.

title: EV rapid-charger cables cut and stolen overnight — hubs down for days and the 99% reliability duty missed
problem: Organised thieves cut copper-rich rapid-charger cables worth only ~£20–£25 in scrap; each cable costs ~£1,000+ to replace, plus days of downtime. InstaVolt reported ~£410k of losses from ~100 incidents, and incidents reportedly doubled in 2024. The Public Charge Point Regulations 2023 require 99% reliability across rapid networks, yet operators often learn of a theft only when drivers complain.
who_suffers: CPO operations teams, drivers, site hosts
buyer: CPO Head of Operations / Field Service Manager
industry: UK rapid and ultra-rapid public EV charging hubs (including forecourt hubs)
current_workaround: CCTV, GPS trackers in cables, police partnerships, reactive repair
sensor_concept: Retrofit cable-holster and cable sensor (continuity loop or accelerometer in the cable sleeve), shock sensor on the charger housing and PIR, LTE-M independent of the charger's comms; instant cut/vandalism alert to security and police, run-over damage detection, incident log for insurers and reliability reporting.
notes: c1/c10 strong (sourced losses, trade press), c4 (PCPR 2023 99% reliability), c2 (incidents now monthly across networks), c6 (O&M contractors, insurers). Risk: charger OEMs could build it in.

title: Rapid-charger air filters clog and fans fail — chargers derate or trip in summer while O&M swaps filters on a calendar
problem: Rapid chargers are air-cooled; clogged intake filters or failed fans cause power derating and thermal trips, cutting revenue and reliability. O&M contractors replace filters on fixed schedules (each visit ~£150–£400) and can't see thermal health when they lack access to OEM data.
who_suffers: CPOs, drivers getting slow charges, O&M contractors
buyer: CPO Asset / Maintenance Manager; O&M contractor
industry: Public rapid EV charging networks and fleet depots
current_workaround: Calendar-based filter swaps; reactive call-outs after drivers report slow charging
sensor_concept: Stick-on sensor at the intake and exhaust grilles measuring differential temperature, fan vibration/acoustic signature and pressure drop, LTE-M; condition-based filter-change scheduling and early fan-failure alerts.
notes: c2 (recurring every summer), c3 (scheduled O&M visits), c6 (O&M contractors), c8 (cheap sensors). c7 risk: OEM telemetry may already report temperatures.

title: Charger shows 'offline' — tripped supply after rain or just a 4G dropout? Engineers dispatched blind
problem: Public and destination chargers often show 'offline' in the CPO back office. Nobody knows whether the supply tripped (needs a reset or an engineer) or the 4G link dropped (the charger still works), so engineers (~£150–£500 per call-out) are dispatched blind or sites stay down for days, hurting reliability metrics under the Public Charge Point Regulations 2023.
who_suffers: CPO operations teams, site hosts (supermarkets, hotels), drivers
buyer: CPO Field Service Manager; site host Facilities Manager
industry: Public and destination EV charging sites
current_workaround: Remote reboot attempts, asking site staff to look, dispatching engineers
sensor_concept: Independent power-presence watchdog in the feeder pillar or charger supply (CT clamps, voltage presence, cabinet humidity/water ingress, door switch) with its own NB-IoT/LTE-M SIM on a different network; tells ops instantly whether the supply tripped or comms failed, and logs trips against weather.
notes: c1 (truck-roll costs), c2 (weekly faults across a network), c4 (PCPR reliability), c6 (O&M contractors/ICPs). c7 needs evidence of a gap versus OCPP diagnostics.

title: Forecourt rollover car wash or jet-wash bay breaks down unseen — the dealer loses a day's wash revenue
problem: Independent forecourt dealers' rollover washes and jet-wash bays break down (pump, brush motor, payment unit) and nobody notices until customers complain. Downtime costs ~£200–£800 a day per wash in lost revenue (US trade sources put tunnel downtime at ~$650 an hour), and older machines have no remote monitoring.
who_suffers: Forecourt dealers and managers; wash service engineers
buyer: Independent Forecourt Dealer / Area Manager
industry: Forecourt rollover and jet-wash bays at independent and dealer-group petrol stations
current_workaround: Staff noticing, customer complaints, OEM service-contract call-outs; telemetry only on the newest machines
sensor_concept: Current clamps on main motors and pumps, a water-flow sensor and a coin/card pulse counter, LTE-M; detects stoppages, abnormal current (brush/pump wear) and revenue anomalies; alerts the dealer and the service contractor.
notes: c1 (revenue per day), c2 (frequent faults), c6 (wash service companies), c8 (non-hazardous area, cheap CTs). c4 weak.

title: Coin-op forecourt air and vacuum machines broken or full — vending operators send route engineers blind
problem: Operators of forecourt air/water and vacuum machines (thousands of units on host sites) send engineers on fixed routes to empty cash and fix faults. A broken machine loses ~£10–£50 a day and annoys the host, while a full coin box stops revenue; older machines have no telemetry.
who_suffers: Vending operators' route engineers, forecourt hosts, drivers
buyer: Vending Operator Operations Director
industry: Forecourt air, water and vacuum vending machine operators
current_workaround: Fixed collection and service routes; host phone calls
sensor_concept: Retrofit board with a compressor/motor current clamp, coin-pulse counter and tamper switch, LTE-M; per-machine status, revenue and coin-box fill, fault alerts and route optimisation.
notes: c5/c6 (the operator is buyer and service channel), c2 (daily), c3 (route labour). c7 risk: newer card-payment machines may already have telemetry; c4 weak.

title: On-street bollard EV chargers hit by vehicles — damage goes unreported, a safety risk until someone complains
problem: Kerbside bollard and pillar chargers installed under council concessions are clipped by vehicles and vandalised. Damaged units can expose live parts or become trip hazards, but damage is found only by residents or periodic inspections; councils and CPOs face liability claims and repair costs of ~£1k–£5k per strike, usually without identifying the vehicle.
who_suffers: CPO field teams, council highway teams, residents
buyer: CPO Operations Manager on council concession contracts; council EV / Highways Officer
industry: On-street residential EV charging (council concessions, LEVI-funded rollouts)
current_workaround: Periodic inspections; resident reports via apps and helplines
sensor_concept: Internal tilt and shock accelerometer plus door/tamper switch, LTE-M independent of the charger's comms; alert on impact or lean, remote isolation request, timestamped incident log for insurance recovery from the driver.
notes: c4 (highway inspection codes, electrical safety), c6 (CPO O&M), c1 (repair + recovery). c2 moderate; c5 council procurement risk.

title: Independent forecourts reconcile wetstock by hand — slow leaks, theft and short deliveries surface weeks late
problem: Petroleum licensing conditions and Environment Agency guidance expect wetstock records and leak detection proportionate to risk, and trade sources say reconciliation must be daily. Many independent dealers still reconcile from dips or by reading the tank-gauge console by hand, so leaks, theft and short deliveries surface weeks later. Clean-up can cost £100k+, trade press cites EA fines of up to ~£20k, and a 0.5% loss on 2m litres a year is ~£14k.
who_suffers: Independent dealers, Petroleum Enforcement Authority officers, the environment
buyer: Independent Forecourt Dealer / Owner-Operator
industry: Independent petrol forecourts with automatic tank gauge (ATG) consoles
current_workaround: Daily manual reconciliation on paper or spreadsheets; some pay a third-party monthly statistical reconciliation service; periodic tank tests
sensor_concept: Non-ATEX data bridge: an RS-232/USB reader on the existing ATG console inside the shop (no new in-tank hardware), with pump sales captured where available and an LTE-M uplink (no forecourt IT changes); automated daily reconciliation, statistical leak detection, delivery verification, records ready for the licensing authority.
notes: c4 (petroleum licence + EA guidance), c2 (daily), c3 (manual reconciliation), c1 (sourced losses and clean-up costs), c6 (forecourt maintenance contractors). c7 risk: wetstock incumbents (Fairbanks, Insite360, Bottomline); gap is independents; only works on sites with ATG consoles.

title: EV charging bays blocked by petrol cars or overstaying EVs — CPO sessions and host revenue share lost
problem: Rapid hubs and destination car parks lose sessions when bays are ICE'd or EVs overstay after charging. Drivers complain widely, and hosts and CPOs lose ~£20–£100 a day per blocked rapid bay. Overstay fees need evidence, and ANPR is costly for small sites.
who_suffers: Drivers, CPOs, host car park operators
buyer: CPO Commercial / Operations Manager; car park operator
industry: Public EV charging bays at retail, leisure and hub sites
current_workaround: Signage, occasional enforcement patrols, ANPR at larger sites
sensor_concept: In-bay magnetometer/radar occupancy puck combined with the charger session state (via a CPO data feed, no host IT), LoRaWAN/LTE-M; detects non-charging occupancy, notifies the parking-enforcement partner with timestamps, utilisation reports.
notes: c1 (lost sessions quantifiable), c2 (daily), c6 (parking enforcement firms already manage these car parks), c10 (driver complaints). c7 risk: parking sensors and ANPR are crowded.

title: Forecourt LPG cylinder-exchange cages run out in cold snaps or get raided — sales lost and deposits unreconciled
problem: Forecourts sell bottled-gas exchange from outdoor cages restocked by the gas distributor on fixed rounds. Cages empty in cold snaps (lost sales and customers driving to rivals), cylinders are stolen from poorly locked cages, and dealers do manual counts to reconcile cylinder deposits with the distributor.
who_suffers: Forecourt dealers, bottled-gas distributors, customers
buyer: Bottled-gas distributor Retail Operations Manager (or the forecourt dealer)
industry: Bottled LPG cylinder exchange at forecourts and convenience stores
current_workaround: Fixed restock rounds, dealer phone orders, manual stock counts
sensor_concept: Cage-door open sensor plus cylinder count from a weighing plinth or ToF sensors (electronics sealed and mounted outside any hazardous-zone boundary), LTE-M; stock level for distributor auto-restock, out-of-hours door-open alert, monthly deposit reconciliation.
notes: c6 (distributor already visits on rounds and owns the cages), c2 (weekly restocks), c5 (distributor ops budget). Risks: LPG zoning around cages must be checked to avoid ATEX; c4 weak; c1 needs sourcing.
